Learning Objectives
Identify signs and symptoms of failed revision total knee arthroplasty.
Determine the appropriate workup for a patient in whom failed revision total knee
arthroplasty is suspected.
Describe salvage procedures for failed revision total knee arthroplasty.
Determine host factors that may guide decision making for appropriate salvage procedures
after failed revision total knee arthroplasty.

Approximately 25% of aseptic total knee arthroplasty (TKA) revisions are re-revised within 10
years.
The true rate of revision TKA failure is difficult to determine.

Incidence of Revision Total Knee Arthroplasty Failure
The most accurate data on failure rates are from national registries. Registry data from
Australia and New Zealand suggest that approximately 25% of aseptic TKA revisions are
re-revised within 10 years.1 However, many registries do not track salvage procedures,
such as arthrodesis or amputation, which makes the true failure rate and incidence of
salvage procedures unclear. Regardless, relatively few patients with an infected TKA
implant (<5%) are thought to eventually undergo to amputation. Using institutional data,
Sierra et al2 reported a 26% and 34% rate of re-revision surgery at 10 years and 15 years,
respectively. Mortazavi et al3 reported an 18% re-revision rate at 10 years, with infection
being the major cause of failure 44%.
In general, revision TKA is a successful procedure; however, arthroplasty surgeons
continue to encounter complex situations of multiple failed revision attempts in patients
for whom limited reconstruction options are available. The surgeon and the patient are
then faced with the question, “When is enough, enough?”. Historically, surgical treatment
options for these difficult scenarios were limited to above-knee amputation (AKA) versus
knee arthrodesis. With advancements in implant technology, surgical techniques, and
experience, limb salvage with the use of tumor-type endoprostheses has been
considered and used for these reconstruction procedures.
Modes of Revision TKA Failure Based on Australian Registry Data
Loosening: 38.3%
Infection: 25.6%
Instability: 8.1%
Trauma/periprosthetic fracture
Extensor mechanism disruption 4


Modes of Revision TKA Failure Based on Australian Registry Data
Revision TKA fails because of the same reasons that primary TKA fails. For example, the
incidence of postoperative periprosthetic femur fracture after revision TKA ranges from
0.3% to 38%. Approximately 11% of patients in whom two-stage revision fails because of
infection are unable to undergo reimplantation, ultimately requiring arthrodesis or AKA.5
Risk Factors for Revision TKA Failure
Dependent on the mode of failure
The postoperative mortality rate is higher in patients who undergo revision for periprosthetic
infection than in patients who undergo revision for aseptic failure.
The risk of readmission is higher in females, patients receiving general anesthesia, and
patients with a preoperative history of transient ischemic attack.
Certain factors (ie, male sex, increased constraint, cardiovascular disease) have been
associated with an increased risk of aseptic revision failure.


Background
Patients in whom distal femur replacement (DFR) is considered typically fall into two
main categories: patients undergoing revision for a previously failed TKA implant with no
remaining bone stock in the distal femur to support preservation of the femoral
condyles and elderly patients with a comminuted distal femur fracture in whom DFR is
performed as a primary arthroplasty procedure. If used for both primary and revision
procedures, DFR affords immediate knee stability for early weight bearing.
DFR results in good outcomes with regard to mobilization, joint function, and limb
salvage; however, studies consistently report a higher rate of complications in
nononcologic settings.7 As described with other megaprostheses, infection is the main
mode of failure for nononcologic DFR, with infection rates as high as 18.5% reported.8
Supracondylar femur fracture is the most common periprosthetic femur fracture after
TKA. For non-reconstructible periprosthetic femur fractures, DFR is a reliable option. In a
series on the use of a megaprosthesis for the management of supracondylar femur
fractures after TKA, Rahman et al9 reported an 89% survival rate for DFR. In a cohort of
31 patients, Chalmers et al10 reported a 97% 5-year survival rate for cemented DFR for
the management of periprosthetic femur fractures in patients with a prior primary TKA
implant; however, the authors reported a substantially reduced 5-year survival rate of
18% for DFR after revision TKA. Additional studies are necessary to adequately assess
the long-term complications and survival of these complex revision procedures
Primary reconstruction via DFR in patients with a periprosthetic femur fracture resulted
in fewer subsequent revision procedures and complications compared with patients with
a periprosthetic femur who underwent DFR after failed open reduction internal fixation.9
Although constrained condylar total knee components are the main options for complex
revision TKA, they may not be a feasible option in patients in whom revision TKA fails.
Berend et al11 assessed DFR for the treatment of patients with severe bone loss and
reported promising results, with revision surgery performed in 13% of patients. Of 37
patients who underwent 39 DFR procedures, two patients had recurrent infections, a

chronic infection occurred in one patient, one patient sustained a periprosthetic
fracture, and one patient had knee hyperextension. At a mean follow-up of 46 months,
aseptic loosening was not observed in any of the patients in the series.
If performing DFR, careful attention to patellar tracking and implant rotation is critical.
Rotation of the tibia is determined by lining up the implant with the medial third of the
tibial tubercle, similar to that in standard TKA; however, after distal femur resection,
femoral rotation may be difficult to assess. In general, the femoral component is placed
in 3° of external rotation to allow for appropriate patellar tracking. The most reliable
method to assess femoral rotation of trial components is with the knee in flexion relative
to the trial tibial component. In extension, alignment of the limb should be noted, and
the surgeon should range the knee through a flexion-extension arc of motion to assess
patellar tracking. Although less of a concern in primary and revision TKA, leg length must
be considered during trialing of distal femur components. If the knee cannot be fully
flexed against gravity when lifting the thigh, the femur may have been overlengthened,
and shorter trial components should be used or the resection should be taken higher if
the smallest construct is being trialed. The nonsurgical extremity should be accessible to
gauge limb length. Surgeons should consider that a bump placed under the hip may
internally rotate the femur. The implant position should then be fine-tuned to ensure
adequate tracking and range of motion. More external rotation is better than internal
rotation. If satisfactory, the surgeon can then mark the implant position on the femur
with the use of electrocautery as a reference for final implant positioning.
Techniques
Preoperative Planning
Contralateral knee radiographs to establish the location of the joint line (approximately 1 cm
distal to the inferior pole of the patella)
Prior surgical notes, including implant information
Evaluation for periprosthetic joint infection
Positioning

Supine on regular table
Thigh tourniquet placed as proximal as possible
Surgical Approach
For revision, use a previous midline incision if possible.
If multiple longitudinal incisions are present, use the most lateral incision.
Allow a 4- to 6-cm bridge between previous incisions.

Surgical Approach
The need for extensile exposure may depend on the extent of the previous surgery. An
extensile medial parapatellar arthrotomy may be attempted for initial exposure. If this is
not adequate, a quadriceps snip may be performed obliquely across the superior aspect
of the quadriceps tendon for additional exposure without affecting postoperative
recovery. In the setting of multiple revisions and considerable scarring/difficult exposure,
a tibial tubercle osteotomy should be considered.
Techniques
Skeletonize the distal femur by performing a transverse osteotomy at the distal aspect of the
femoral diaphysis, preserving as much length necessary to accommodate the implant.
Mark distal femur rotation before the osteotomy.
Ream at least 10 to 15 cm up the femoral diaphysis.
Prepare the tibia via standard techniques (bone-preserving DFR for a fracture, revision
techniques for failed TKA).
Place the trial components.
Perform joint line restoration based on the inferior pole of the patella,1 cm from the inferior
pole.
Assess rotation with the knee flexed 90° (Figure 1).
Use the tension of the surrounding soft-tissue envelope and tracking of the patella to guide
rotation of the femoral and tibial implants, which may be difficult.
After rotation is set, mark the spot on the femur.


Techniques
Final femoral implant placement should be performed via a fully cemented technique:
placement of a cement restrictor, pressurized cement placement, and implant
placement. Hybrid femoral fixation techniques have been reported, whereas the tibial
implant may be placed in a hybrid or fully cemented fashion. Fixation should be based
on implant characteristics, bone stock, and surgeon preference.
Postoperative Management
Immediate weight bearing as tolerated: This may differ if a tibial tubercle osteotomy was
performed. No change in the postoperative regimen is necessary with a quadriceps snip.
Mechanical and chemical deep vein thrombosis prophylaxis
Early range of motion
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Management of medical comorbidities during DFR is crucial because many patients
undergoing the procedure are frail and have multiple comorbidities. Preoperative and
postoperative medical optimization is key to minimizing complications.
A knee immobilizer may be considered in the immediate postoperative period to minimize fall
risk.

Background

Background
Allograft-prosthetic composite (APC), also referred to as structural allograft, typically
consists of a stemmed femoral or tibial component cemented to an allograft, which then
is fixed to host bone. This option may be advantageous in younger patients if the goal is
to restore previously lost bone stock in anticipation of potential future revision surgery.
In older patients, distal femur (or proximal tibia) replacement may be a more
appropriate treatment option because success with APC depends on incorporation of
the allograft bone with the host. Young patients with a large, uncontained defect that
cannot be overcome with the use of metal augments and polyethylene inserts in whom
bone stock preservation/restoration is a priority are ideal candidates for APC.
The results of APC/structural allograft generally are favorable, with 5-year survivorship
rates ranging from 67% to 92% and nonunion rates being less than 4%. Infection rates
range from zero to 15%, which is consistent with other revision and salvage techniques.


Indications
Smaller defects typically are managed with morcellized bone, cement, or metal
augments. This strategy may be more useful in younger patients, who likely will undergo
restoration of bone stock for future revision surgery. The amount of bone loss can be
categorized according to the severity of the bone defects and whether they are
contained (ie, defined by a circumferential rim of cortical bone) or uncontained (Tables 2
and 3).


Contraindications
Use of APC is associated with a unique set of contraindications. Because the
effectiveness of the composite depends on healing of graft bone to host bone, any

condition in which bone healing is compromised represents a contraindication. Previous
irradiation, smoking, and use of medications that impede bone healing warrant caution.
Techniques
Preoperative Planning
Infection must be ruled out via a combination of inflammatory serum and joint fluid laboratory
tests, joint aspiration cell count, differential blood count, and cultures.
Size matching of the allograft is preferred.
Fresh-frozen (rather than freeze-dried) allografts have superior structural integrity, specifically
against torsional forces.
Positioning

Positioning
Patient positioning and surgical approach are similar to those of any revision TKA
procedure. The patient should be placed in the supine position. Previous midline
incisions should be used if possible. Maximum exposure is critical to fully delineate the
extent of the bony defect. A low threshold should exist for the use of extensile
techniques, including a quadriceps snip and/or tibial tubercle osteotomy.
Surgical Technique
To clearly delineate bone defects, all previous implants and diseased tissue, including all
nonviable bone, tissue, and cement, should be removed after exposure.
Femoral epicondyles should be preserved with collateral ligament attachments if possible
(Figure 2).
Perform a step cut of the host bone for rotational stability.

Proximal tibia
Similar to the distal femur, ream the host canal for 5 cm of press fit beyond the graft-host
junction.
Use step cuts to fit the graft to the host bone.
The goal is to restore the anatomic joint line (tibial implant plus polyethylene 1.5 to 2 cm
above the top of the proximal fibula).
Make a proximal tibial cut of the allograft and insert the trial component.
Determine rotation using a patellar/extensor mechanism. Mark it using a pen for later
alignment (Figure 3).
Implantation of components
Principles: uncemented fixation in the host bone, cemented fixation in the allograft
First, fix the implants to the graft bone with the use of cement.
After the cement has cured, press-fit the implant to the host bone.
Earlier literature suggested the use of plates and/or screws for supplementation21 (Resource
1).
However, this is not currently recommended because it may compromise structural integrity
and, potentially, lead to graft resorption.
The sutures previously placed through the graft at the sites of the medial and lateral
epicondyles are then brought through the host epicondyles and secured to the graft with the
knee in 90°of flexion.
Use a minimal level of constraint based on the integrity of the epicondyles/collateral
ligaments (posterior stabilized at a minimum).
Postoperative Management
Early range of motion
Restrictions based on exposure (ie, if tibial tubercle osteotomy is performed, restrict active
extension for 6 weeks postoperatively)
Limited weight bearing until radiographic evidence of graft union (3 months postoperatively)
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Preoperative planning is critical to assess the soft-tissue envelope, confirm the absence of
infection, etc.
Schedule a preoperative plastic surgery consultation if wound/coverage concerns exist.

Avoid cement extrusion in the graft-host interface (will lead to nonunion).
Use matching step cuts to prevent malrotation.

Arthrodesis
Indications
Many classic indications for knee arthrodesis exist:
Unilateral posttraumatic osteoarthritis in a young patient
Knee with multiple surgical procedures
Painful pseudarthrosis
Neuropathic arthritis
Paralytic conditions (ie, polio)
Posttumor resection
However, this lesson focuses on knee arthrodesis in patients in whom TKA fails because of:
Persistent and recalcitrant infection after multiple attempts at eradication via surgery and
antibiotic agents
Chronic extensor mechanism disruption in the setting of infection
Catastrophic soft tissues, such as those requiring free flaps about the knee if another
arthroplasty procedure were to be performed
A desire to avoid future revision arthroplasty
Contraindications

Contraindications
A patient who cannot tolerate the limitations inherent to knee arthrodesis may require
other treatment options (eg, chronic antibiotic suppression or amputation).
To determine whether a patient can tolerate arthrodesis, a cylinder cast or brace can be
applied and positioned as if for arthrodesis (ie, as a trial). This will allow the patient to
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:08 PM
AAOS | Salvage Procedures and Failed Revision Total Knee Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000023
17/35

experience the limitations of arthrodesis (eg, driving, traveling, and ambulation) before
committing to the procedure.
Contraindications to intramedullary fixation include ipsilateral total hip arthroplasty,
substantial femoral or tibial deformity, and continued active infection22 (Resource 2).
Multiple studies have reported promising results with arthrodesis as a salvage treatment
option. In a study of 165 patients in Denmark, Gottsfriedsen et al23 reported that bony
fusion was achieved in 65% of the patients after arthrodesis. In this cohort,
intramedullary nailing resulted in greater fusion rates than external fixation. Failed
arthrodesis occurred in 24% of patients, who ultimately required an AKA. Bargiotas et
al24 reported successful fusion in 10 of 12 patients who underwent staged arthrodesis.
The mean time to union was 5.5 months, and the mean leg-length discrepancy was 5.5
cm. Arthrodesis failed in two patients, one of whom sustained a broken implant and one
of whom underwent conversion to an AKA.
In a retrospective review of data on a cohort of 43 patients at a single institution,
Schwarzkopf et al25reported a 75% fusion rate. Failed procedures occurred in six
patients, four of whom required repeat arthrodesis and two of whom required an AKA.
The authors reported that the patients in whom arthrodesis was successful had a lower
preoperative erythrocyte sedimentation rate, a lower rate of wound complications, and a
shorter hospital length of stay compared with the patients in whom arthrodesis failed.
Poor outcomes also have been demonstrated for arthrodesis after TKA. In a cohort of 26
patients, Röhner et al26 reported that 50% of the patients had a persistent infection
requiring revision surgery and 73% of the patients had persistent pain. The authors
concluded that arthrodesis afforded poor quality of life and were strongly opposed to
recommending the procedure.
Given the dilemma of arthrodesis versus AKA, patients have better functional outcomes
and improved ambulation after arthrodesis;22 however, patients who undergo
arthrodesis have a higher rate of postoperative infections, with Carr et al27 reporting a
postoperative infection rate of 14.5% for arthrodesis versus 8.3% for AKA. The overall
health of the patient also should be considered in comparing these treatment options.

The metabolic demands of an AKA are considerable, and patients with poor
cardiovascular reserve may have considerable difficulties with prosthesis fitting and
ambulation.28
Techniques
Preoperative Planning
Arthrodesis should be planned with the following end goals:
0° to 5° valgus
Limb shortening: Assists in relaxing hamstrings for hip flexibility and aids in activities of daily
living. Limb shortening is inevitable with arthrodesis after TKA because the space previously
occupied by implants has been removed. Classically, arthrodesis was performed with 10° to
15° of knee flexion to shorten the limb. This degree of flexion is unnecessary if arthrodesis is
performed for failed TKA because the limb will already be shortened.
Positioning
Typically, supine position
Surgical Approaches
Regardless of technique, the previous midline incisions from revision arthroplasty are used if
possible.
Techniques
Multiple techniques are available for arthrodesis:
External dynamic compression
Intramedullary nail fixation
Technique for intramedullary nail fixation
Full-length radiographs are necessary for preoperative planning for intramedullary nail length
and canal diameter.
Patient supine on a radiolucent table
Bump under hip to assess greater trochanter starting point

Leg prepared from above iliac crest down to foot
Next, sequential reaming up to 2 mm greater than the nail diameter is performed. This is
performed in a retrograde fashion in the femur and in an antegrade fashion in the tibia.
The lengths of the femur and tibia are measured from inside the joint and are added to
determine nail length.
The guidewire is then passed up the femur in a retrograde fashion and retrieved through the
piriformis fossa.
After the guidewire has been retrieved, the opening reamer is placed over the guidewire to
prepare for nail insertion.
Nail passage to the level of the knee
Reduce the tibia to the femur, maintaining rotation as marked previously.
The nail is advanced approximately 2 to 6 cm proximal to the tibial plafond and locked distally,
after which back slapping is performed to achieve compression at the arthrodesis site.
Bone grafting of the knee is then performed to encourage healing at the arthrodesis site.
After compression has been obtained, interlocking screws are placed proximally and in a
standard fashion (Figures 4 and 5).

Techniques
Currently, the most common nailing arthrodesis technique involves the use of a long
antegrade nail. This is the preferred technique of the authors of this lesson; however,
intramedullary nail fixation also can be performed with the use of modular or
nonmodular nails. Modular nails are associated with the advantage of placement
through the knee incision (ie, without accessory incisions), and some designs may
provide dynamic compression. Short modular designs also can be used in patients with
ipsilateral hip or distal tibial implants; however, removal may be difficult.22
Compression plate fixation: This method is less common than nail fixation because it
requires wider exposure and because bone quality often is poor, making screw purchase
difficult. In addition, the rate of union after knee arthrodesis is lower with external
fixation devices (and with all other techniques described) than with intramedullary nail
fixation.22
The nail should extend from the tip of the greater trochanter to approximately 2 cm
from the tibial plafond. Any bone being resected must be accounted for in templating
nail length.

The procedure begins by accessing the knee joint. Before old components are removed,
the anterior femur and tibia should be marked for rotational alignment. The
components are then removed, and thorough débridement is performed. Fresh cuts are
made on the femoral and tibial surfaces. If the quality of the patella is sufficient, it can be
preserved and used as a bone graft.
Postoperative Management
Weight bearing as tolerated
Postoperative dressings based on surgeon discretion; may consider incisional negative
pressure wound therapy
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Thorough débridement is critical and should include any cement and chronic inflammatory
tissue that may impede healing at the arthrodesis site.
Proper rotation is key. Rotation should be assessed in multiple ways before final interlocking
screw placement.
Above-Knee Amputation
Background

Background
If salvage procedures ultimately fail, the final stage and solution likely is AKA. AKA is
exceedingly rare, with an incidence of 0.03% to 0.36% after TKA.29 An AKA increases the
energy expenditure of ambulation, which ultimately may result in poor function and
limited ambulation. Multiple studies have demonstrated that less than 50% of patients
have functional mobility after undergoing an AKA for failed TKA.30,31
In the study performed over a 30-year period, Sierra et al29 reported that 0.36% (67
patients) of more than 18,000 patients who underwent TKA necessitated an AKA. Of
these 67 patients, 25 patients required an AKA for reasons attributed to the index

More than one-quarter of these patients sustained wound complications. Of the nine
patients who were fitted for a prosthesis, only five patients were walking at the time of
last follow-up. Similarly, in a study by Fedorka et al,30 only 23% of patients were
functionally independent in the community after AKA.
The authors reported that 9 of 35 patients required subsequent irrigation and
débridement for wound complications after AKA and two patients underwent repeat
AKA
Suboptimal outcomes of AKA were further demonstrated in a multicenter study of 111
patients by Ryan et al.31 The authors reported that, in the 94% of individuals who owned
a prosthesis, only 56% used the prosthesis, 56% primarily used a wheelchair, and 47%
were being treated with chronic pain medications. Phantom pain was reported in 80% of
the patients, and only 53% of patients were satisfied with the procedure. However,
Khanna et al32 reported good results after AKA for failed TKA. The authors reported that
all the patients were satisfied with AKA after recurrent periprosthetic joint infections,
and six of seven patients said they wished they would have decided to undergo
amputation earlier. Improved quality of life is observed in patients who are fitted for a
prosthesis and able to ambulate, which is associated with younger age and fewer
comorbidities.30
AKA should be considered if salvage procedures have failed. AKA is the most radical
treatment option for the multiply revised, failed TKA implant. Patients who undergo AKA
should be counseled preoperatively on the insult to functional status; however, younger
patients in whom future prosthetic fitting is likely may benefit from earlier conversion to
AKA given the lengthy physical and psychological recovery process inherent to the
procedure. Patients in whom AKA is being considered in comparison with other
treatment options (arthrodesis) should talk with other patients who have undergone
AKA to develop more realistic goals and expectations after this last-resort procedure

Contraindications
If a patient can tolerate a limb-saving procedure, it should be considered. Elective amputation
requires extensive patient counseling about expectations.
Techniques
Preoperative Planning
The planned amputation level should be distal enough to maximize function while eradicating
infection.
Maximizing length will improve sitting balance and prosthesis fit.
Dead space must be managed via muscle transposition.
In patients with chronic infection, amputation may need to be performed in stages.
Techniques
Patient positioning: supine with a bump under the buttock of the surgical side to allow for hip
extension and adduction during the procedure
Mark skin flaps (Figure 7).
Ideal resection level is 10 to 15 cm above the knee joint for maximal prosthesis fit; however,
most patients undergoing AKA for failed revision TKA will be using a wheelchair.
After femoral vessels have been identified in the adductor canal and the adductor tendon has
been detached for myodesis, the vessels should be ligated at the level of the bone resection.
Major nerves should be cut sharply 4 cm proximal to the planned bone resection.

An incisional negative pressure wound dressing should be applied. The residual limb can then
be wrapped with the use of an elastic bandage or stump shrinker.
The patient should be mobilized in a wheelchair and work on upper body strength.
A prosthesis fitting should be done as soon as soft-tissue healing allows.
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Nerves can be infiltrated with local anesthetic at the time of surgery to minimize postoperative
pain.
The development of appropriate soft-tissue flaps will minimize the risk of wound breakdown.
Complications

Complications
Most complications related to transfemoral amputation are similar to those of any
amputation and include infection, heterotopic ossification, phantom pain, wound
breakdown, and neuroma formation. Complications unique to transfemoral amputation
is abductor drift, which is unopposed pull of the abductors because of ineffective
adductor myodesis. This can be avoided by using the previously described technique to
perform adductor myodesis.
Outcomes
Risk factors for failure
Knee arthrodesis versus AKA for failed revision of infected TKA (Resource 3)
Patients who undergo arthrodesis have higher rates of infection and transfusion than
patients who undergo AKA, whereas patients who undergo AKA have higher rates of systemic
complications and in-hospital mortality than patients who undergo arthrodesis.27
DFR versus APC (Resource 4)
According to one study of treatment options for the management of periprosthetic distal
femur fractures,33 patients who underwent DFR had shorter surgical time and less blood loss
than patients who underwent APC. Short-term functional outcomes were similar.33
